title: Structured Visuo-Semantic Perception
summary: Mirage removes prose construction from visual perception and uses spatial heads, region references and compact semantic fields.
body_markdown:
When an agent looks through a camera, it needs the objects, their positions, the writing and the relationships between them. A sentence is one way to carry that information, but composing the sentence is an additional job. The model must choose an order, connect clauses, resolve references and decide how much explanation to give. A small model running on a phone has a limited budget for all of this.


Our argument is that prose construction, verbose semantic descriptions and open-ended reasoning spend capacity that a perception model could use on the image itself. Mirage removes those requirements and introduces structural bias into the problem. It predicts geometry with spatial heads, reads text with a dedicated reader and expresses meaning through compact fields and references. We call this structured visuo-semantic perception.


This article follows that division of work through the released model, from pixels to the record an application receives. The[Mirage release post](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/mirage) has the runnable examples and device measurements.


## Remove the prose, keep the meaning


Consider a model describing a red stop sign mounted on a black pole. A paragraph might introduce the sign, add a clause about its colour, connect the pole with “which” or “and”, then explain where both sit in the scene. An application has to recover the entities and their connections from that paragraph.


Mirage gives the sign and pole names and properties, then records` attached_to` as a relation between their IDs. The relation still matters. What disappears is the need to compose it into a sentence, maintain a narrative and repeat enough context for a human reader to follow it.


The distinction is between semantic content and its verbal packaging. Removing conjunctions does not mean removing logical conjunction, negation or relationships. Two properties can coexist in a record without a sentence joining them. A relation has explicit endpoints instead of a pronoun whose referent the next component must infer. Open-vocabulary values still allow the model to name and describe things beyond a fixed class list.


The same principle applies to reasoning. Mirage exposes a short generated trace, but its perception interface does not ask for an essay or an unrestricted chain of thought. Decisions can be bounded by a supplied set of choices or a form. A system that needs broader deliberation can use the resulting record as input to an agent.

The spatial heads provide proposals and masks. Proposals guide the reader's crops and the decoder's region slots. The runtime combines their outputs into a record. Read strings are not fed back into the semantic decoder.


The structure enters at three levels. Spatial heads restrict how geometry is produced. Region references restrict how a semantic item attaches to that geometry. The output format restricts how the description is expressed. Reducing prose alone would leave the first two problems with the language decoder.

Shared prototypes combined with instance coefficients are the construction introduced by[YOLACT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.02689) . It imposes a limit as well. Before thresholding and box restriction, each mask logit map lies in the span of 32 prototypes. OCR has a different geometry from object naming. Small characters need local detail that may be lost when the whole image is resized. Its job is narrower than generating a free-form answer. It writes a compact line representation for scene fields, entities, text references, relations and events. The runtime expands those lines into JSON and resolves region references into geometry. Names and property values remain open vocabulary. The structure is fixed enough for the application to consume without recovering it from prose.


This still leaves real sequence problems. The decoder chooses which semantic items to mention and when to stop. It can repeat items, omit a visible object or assign an incorrect relationship. Moving geometry into a head removes coordinate generation from that sequence; it does not remove the sequence itself.

## What the structure saves


There are two distinct budgets. The first is representational capacity. A fixed spatial head and a region-reference interface limit the family of computations the model must express through language. This is our reason for imposing the bias. The second is inference work. Coordinates, mask contours and OCR strings no longer all consume decoder steps, and compact fields avoid sentence construction and repeated connective language.

A shorter output is therefore evidence of less decoding, not by itself evidence of a proportional end-to-end speedup or better perception.


Structural bias also restricts what can be expressed. A 64-proposal budget is finite. A missed proposal cannot be recovered merely by selecting a different reference. Shared masks have limited spatial detail. A compact record is suitable for perception and bounded decisions, while a conversational explanation asks more of the system. We chose the interface around what a local agent needs from its camera.


## Where this sits among vision models


The boundary is not simply detectors on one side and language models on the other.[Grounding DINO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05499) already supports open-set, language-conditioned detection.[Florence-2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.06242) expresses several vision tasks through a sequence interface, including detection and segmentation. Groma and ChatRex explicitly connect proposed regions with language. These systems establish that open vocabulary, structure and grounding can be combined in several ways.


Mirage's design choice is to make a compact perception record the main interface and assign its fields to computations suited to their geometry. HConvGLU reduces the cost of channel mixing inside the encoder; the[HConvGLU article](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/hconvglu) derives that operator separately. Structural perception concerns a different level of the design, namely what the model is asked to produce and which part produces it.


## Measure the fields and their connections


A useful evaluation must check both the individual predictions and how they attach to one another. Box recall alone cannot establish grounded naming, and correct names cannot establish localisation.


Part of the result What to measure


Object proposals Precision and recall at stated IoU thresholds and proposal budgets


Grounded names Name correctness on geometrically matched regions


Instance masks Mask overlap for matched instances, including small objects


Read text Character and word errors on matched text regions


Attributes and scene fields Correct, contradicted and missing facts


Relations Predicate correctness with both endpoints matched


Decisions Accuracy and probability calibration for a stated choice set


Runtime End-to-end latency with image size, output sections, precision and device specified


To isolate the capacity argument, a comparison needs matched model budgets and evaluation conditions while varying the semantic format and the division of work. Release latency establishes that this implementation runs at a particular speed. It does not isolate how much of its quality comes from removing prose, using region references or changing the encoder.

If you already have a language model in your application, can Mirage give it enough visual context to answer questions about a photo? This is a useful test of the interface. The perception model has to preserve the facts another model needs, and the language model has to use them without seeing the image.

Composing vision and language through text has a clear precedent in[Socratic Models](https://socraticmodels.github.io/) . Our experiment concerns the particular boundary Mirage provides, a small perception model returning named fields, regions and relationships that an existing text model can consume.


### The experiment


We ran the experiment locally on 5 November 2026. The final comparison uses **256 questions from 128 COCO images in VQAv2 validation** , with two questions per image. We selected images and questions by a fixed hash ordering, before generating their predictions. These images are disjoint from the 128-image development sample used to settle the prompt and answer format.


Mirage saw the image but neither question. It returned scene fields, named objects and regions, descriptions, counts, boxes, scores, OCR, relations, events and the complete generated trace. We omitted masks and points from this text interface. All five conditions reuse the same perception result. We did not repair its names, coordinates, duplicate entities or read strings.


Qwen used its original BF16 weights through MLX on an Apple M5 Max. Thinking mode was disabled, decoding was greedy, and each response had a 64-token limit. Every condition used the same instruction to return a JSON object containing a short` answer` . We parsed that field with` json.loads` , without a judge model or response repair. The exact prompt, model revisions, file hashes and dependencies are in the[protocol](https://www.cactuscompute.com/experiments/mirage-qwen/protocol.json) and[runtime record](https://www.cactuscompute.com/experiments/mirage-qwen/runtime.json) .


The five inputs were the question alone, the question with only` scene` , the structured record without` reasoning` , the record with the complete trace, and the complete record from the next distinct image in the frozen sample order. This last condition keeps real visual descriptions in the prompt while breaking their connection to the question's image.

The matched record with its trace beat the mismatched record by **9.0 points** . A paired bootstrap over images, keeping both questions together in each of 10,000 resamples, gives a 95% interval of **4.9 to 13.2 points** . This is evidence that the correct visual context helped on this sample. The mismatched score also shows why the question-only comparison is insufficient. A plausible but irrelevant record can still change the model's guesses and answer format.


The other differences need more restraint. Adding the trace changed the score by **−1.8 points** , with an interval of **−5.0 to 1.2** . We did not find a reliable benefit from passing it along. The record with its trace exceeded scene fields by 3.1 points, but that interval also crossed zero, from −1.1 to 7.2. This experiment does not isolate the value of JSON syntax or compare structure against a prose description containing exactly the same facts.

```text

```


Three cases selected after scoring to illustrate a useful answer, missing information and a trace-dependent error. The complete fixed sample is available below. VQA credit measures agreement with the reference answers, not confidence.


For the wine photo, Mirage names a wine bottle and glasses. Qwen answers` wine` from the structured record, while scene fields alone lead to` none` . The description still contains errors, including the table material and duplicated reflections. A useful answer does not validate every field.


The skateboard photo shows the opposite outcome. Mirage misses the skateboard and returns several cars, people and shoes. Qwen guesses` a skateboard` from the question alone, then answers` a car` when given the record and trace. Extra context can be worse than a language prior when it omits the relevant object and introduces distractions.


The television example makes the trace comparison tangible. The record contains a silver` antenna` , but also calls the television a` digital scale` . Without the trace, Qwen answers` antenna` . Adding the trace changes its answer to` digital scale` . We can observe that change without treating either generated trace as a faithful explanation of the model's internal computation.


Answer format remains a limitation even with valid JSON. Qwen sometimes puts a complete sentence inside` answer` . For example,` Yes, the animals have stripes.` receives zero credit against` yes` , despite agreeing in meaning. The score therefore measures the complete answering interface, including brevity and wording, rather than visual understanding alone. All 1,280 final responses were valid JSON. One question-only reply reached the 64-token limit and was retained.


We encountered this problem during development. An initial prompt containing coordinate definitions sometimes caused Qwen to echo those definitions. A shorter prompt often produced sentences instead of short answers. We retained[both development runs](https://www.cactuscompute.com/experiments/mirage-qwen/README.md) , checked the JSON format on the separate release photo, then froze it before running the fresh comparison above. This was an exploration with prompt development, not a preregistered benchmark.


The final sample contains 90 yes/no questions, 35 number questions and 131 other questions. With the trace included, their scores were 61.3, 21.4 and 13.2 respectively. There is considerable room for improvement in detail retrieval and counting. We did not audit overlap with either model's training data, and this table is not a comparison against a native VLM. The result supports a working composition on this sample, not a claim that a text boundary preserves every visual capability.


We also tried larger text-only readers with the same prompt and records. They did not produce consistent gains. Qwen3-4B Instruct improved on the smaller reader, but its gain over answering without visual context remained uncertain. Qwen3-1.7B and Nemotron 3 Nano 4B often failed the answer-format contract. The[follow-up record](https://www.cactuscompute.com/experiments/mirage-qwen/README.md) retains every condition, failed response and confidence interval. These runs give us reasons to examine the interface more carefully before making a stronger claim.


### Try the connection


The[experiment bundle](https://www.cactuscompute.com/experiments/mirage-qwen/experiment.zip) contains the runner, a standalone` ask.py` , the fixed questions, all observations and responses, and the scoring results. On Apple Silicon, in an environment with Python 3.12, the example runs with


```text
pip   install   -r   requirements.txt
python   ask.py   photo.jpg   "What drink is shown?"
```


The essential boundary is small. The runnable example passes this context and the question through Qwen's chat template, then calls the unchanged text model.


```text
import   json
import   cactus


vision   =   cactus.Mirage()
observations   =   vision.describe(
"photo.jpg"  ,
fields  =  [  "bbox"  ,   "score"  ,   "position"  ,   "description"  ,   "count"  ],
)
context   =   json.dumps(observations,   ensure_ascii  =  False  )
```


On this machine, warm Mirage calls had a median of **77.5 ms** on CPU. Qwen's subsequent answer call had a median of **60.0 ms** on the Metal GPU with the full trace. These are separately measured stages, excluding downloads and model loading. They are not an end-to-end pipeline benchmark. The median full prompt contained 586 tokens. The 22 MB size belongs to Mirage alone; Qwen's BF16 weights are additional.

That boundary lets an application inspect the observations, decide which fields it needs and change its language model independently. The next test should ask which facts the record consistently loses, and whether a targeted second look can recover them. A larger language model may read a record better, but it still needs the relevant visual evidence to be there.
